intro: Welcome! At work and in daily life you write emails all the time: to your boss, a client, a hotel, a teacher or a friend. Today you learn the parts of a clear email, how to ask for things politely in writing, and how to sound right for a friend or for someone you don't know well.
teachingNotes: Build on a2-short-messages, don't re-teach it: the learner already writes a four-part message to a friend (Hi Sari! → news → a question back → See you soon, Rina) and knows the friend-or-boss switch (Dear Pak Hasan, / Thank you very much / no emoji / Best wishes, or Kind regards,). This lesson goes further: the full semi-formal email in seven parts, in this order: subject line (3–8 words that name the topic: 'Question about the TOEIC evening course', not empty, not 'Hello', not 'URGENT!!!', not the whole message) → greeting → opening line with the purpose → body (short paragraphs) → a clear request → closing line → sign-off + name. Stress that the purpose comes FIRST: Indonesian formal letters put it late (Dengan hormat, / Saya yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini …), English emails say why in the first line.

Greetings and endings. Dear + Mr / Ms + SURNAME (family name): 'Dear Mr Brown,' for Michael Brown, not *'Dear Mr Michael'. Ms (said 'miz') is safe for any woman; Mrs = married, Miss = young or unmarried. Many Indonesian names have no surname, so 'Dear Pak Budi,' / 'Dear Bu Ani,' (from A2) is normal with Indonesian colleagues. No name: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' (very formal) or 'Dear Customer Service team,'. Opening lines: I'm writing to ask about + topic / I'm writing to let you know that … / I'm writing about …; replying: Thank you for your email. Closing lines: I look forward to hearing from you. (look forward to + -ing: a phrase to remember; *'look forward to hear' is the classic error) / Let me know if you have any questions. / Thank you for your help. Sign-offs: Best regards, / Kind regards, / Best wishes, (with s: *'Best regard' is a very common slip in Indonesian offices). 'Mr Brown' (British) = 'Mr. Brown' (American).

Polite requests in writing (the node's common error: *'I want to ask the schedule. Send me soon.' → 'I would like to ask about the schedule. Could you send it to me, please?'). The reader can't hear a friendly voice, so an order (Send me …) or 'I want …' sounds rude; word-for-word 'Mohon segera dikirim' and 'Kindly send …' are still orders. Teach: Could you + base verb …? (recap from a2-can-could: could here is not past, just softer); Would you mind + -ing? (a phrase: *'Would you mind to send' ✗; the polite answer 'No, not at all' means 'no problem, I'll do it'); I would like / I'd like to ask about + topic (ask about = menanyakan tentang; ask for = meminta; 'ask the price / the time / the way' are fine fixed phrases, so never mark them wrong, but 'ask the schedule / the training / the parking' is the Indonesian 'menanyakan jadwal' trap); I'd be grateful if you could + base verb (very polite, for a bigger favour or a stranger: a phrase to remember, don't explain it as a conditional). Softeners: please, just (Could you just check …?), a little (a little later), when you have a moment, if possible. A clear request also says what and when (by Thursday).

Personal vs semi-formal. Personal (friends, family): Hi / Hey, contractions everywhere (I'm, can't), Thanks so much!, Can you …?, an emoji or two, Guess what?, Can't wait to see you!, Love, / Take care, / See you soon, / Cheers, (British, informal). Semi-formal (boss, client, hotel, school, a company): Dear …, I hope you are well, fewer contractions (full forms in the key lines with someone new: I am writing … / I would like …; I'm is fine with a colleague you know well: never mark a contraction wrong in a semi-formal email), Thank you for …, no emoji, no thx / pls / btw / u, polite requests, Best regards,. Indonesian email habits to name: 'Kepada Yth. … Dengan hormat,' → only one greeting line, Dear Mr …, (there is no English line for Dengan hormat; *'With respect,' ✗); 'Mohon maaf mengganggu waktunya' → usually leave it out ('Sorry to bother you' only when you really interrupt someone, e.g. on a day off); 'Terima kasih atas perhatiannya' → 'Thank you for your time.' / 'Thank you for your help.' ('Thank you for your attention' sounds like the end of a presentation); 'Hormat saya,' → Best regards,.

Grammar the learner can use: all A0–A2 grammar plus the chain: although / however / because of / due to / so that / in order to (b1-linkers-contrast-purpose: 'due to' and 'in order to' suit work emails), must / have to / had to / be allowed to / might (b1-modals-advice), I think / In my opinion / I agree (b1-giving-opinions). Limits: no formal letters (Yours faithfully / Yours sincerely: if asked, say they belong to very formal letters, mainly British); no passive ('Please find attached' → teach 'I've attached …'); no indirect questions (Could you tell me when the course starts? comes in b1-indirect-questions-tags: accept a correct one, don't teach the word order); no relative clauses; no second conditional ('I'd be grateful if you could' is a fixed phrase). Typed answers are lowercased and stripped of punctuation when checked, so capitals and commas can't be graded in the checkpoint: give feedback on them (comma after the greeting and the sign-off, name on a new line) in the free email practice. When the learner writes a full email, praise the structure first, then correct ONE thing (usually the request or the sign-off).

keyPoints.title: The parts of an email, with the purpose first
keyPoints.explanation: A semi-formal email has seven parts, in this order: a short subject line that names the topic, a greeting (Dear Mr / Ms + surname,), an opening line that says why you're writing (I'm writing to ask about … / to let you know that …), the body, a clear request, a closing line (I look forward to hearing from you. / Let me know if you have any questions.) and a sign-off with your name (Best regards, / Kind regards, / Best wishes,). Say your purpose in the first line.

id.title: Bagian-bagian email, dengan tujuan di depan
id.explanation: Email semi-formal punya tujuh bagian, dengan urutan ini: baris subjek singkat yang menyebut topiknya, salam pembuka (Dear Mr / Ms + nama keluarga,), kalimat pembuka yang menjelaskan kenapa kamu menulis (I'm writing to ask about … / to let you know that …), isi, permintaan yang jelas, kalimat penutup (I look forward to hearing from you. / Let me know if you have any questions.) dan salam penutup dengan namamu (Best regards, / Kind regards, / Best wishes,). Sampaikan tujuanmu di baris pertama.

keyPoints.title: Polite requests in writing
keyPoints.explanation: In an email the reader can't hear your friendly voice, so an order (Send me …) or I want … sounds rude. Ask with Could you + base verb …?, Would you mind + -ing …?, I would like to ask about + topic, or the very polite phrase I'd be grateful if you could + base verb. Softeners make it kinder: please, just, a little, when you have a moment.

examples.en: Could you send me the timetable, please?
examples.id: Bisakah Anda mengirimkan jadwalnya kepada saya?

examples.en: Would you mind checking these numbers?
examples.id: Apakah Anda keberatan mengecek angka-angka ini?

examples.en: I would like to ask about the training schedule.

id.title: Permintaan yang sopan secara tertulis
id.explanation: Di email, pembaca tidak bisa mendengar nada suaramu yang ramah, jadi perintah (Send me …) atau I want … terdengar kasar. Mintalah dengan Could you + kata kerja dasar …?, Would you mind + -ing …?, I would like to ask about + topik, atau ungkapan yang sangat sopan I'd be grateful if you could + kata kerja dasar. Kata pelunak membuatnya lebih ramah: please, just, a little, when you have a moment.

keyPoints.title: Personal or semi-formal?
keyPoints.explanation: To a friend (personal): Hi …!, contractions like I'm and can't, Thanks so much!, Can you …?, an emoji, Take care, or See you soon,. To a boss, a client, a hotel or a school (semi-formal): Dear …, full words, fewer contractions, Thank you for …, no emoji or chat short forms, Best regards,. Don't translate Indonesian letter habits: Dengan hormat has no English line, and Terima kasih atas perhatiannya is Thank you for your time.

examples.en: Thanks so much for the photos! 😊
Thank you for sending the photos.

examples.id: Terima kasih atas waktu Anda (bukan 'Thank you for your attention').

id.title: Personal atau semi-formal?
id.explanation: Untuk teman (personal): Hi …!, bentuk singkat seperti I'm dan can't, Thanks so much!, Can you …?, satu emoji, Take care, atau See you soon,. Untuk atasan, klien, hotel atau sekolah (semi-formal): Dear …, kata-kata lengkap, lebih sedikit bentuk singkat, Thank you for …, tanpa emoji atau singkatan chat, Best regards,. Jangan menerjemahkan kebiasaan surat Indonesia: Dengan hormat tidak punya padanan dalam bahasa Inggris, dan Terima kasih atas perhatiannya menjadi Thank you for your time.

assessment.prompt: You're writing to the manager of a hotel in Bali, Mr David Wilson. You have never met him. Write the greeting of your email (a comma is optional).
acceptableAnswers: dear mr wilson
dear mister wilson
assessment.rubric: Correct: Dear Mr Wilson (Mr. Wilson in American English; Dear + Mr + surname). 'Dear Mr David Wilson' = 70 (understood, but the first name isn't needed). 'Dear Sir' = 60 (you know his name, so use it). 'Dear David' = 50 (too familiar for someone you've never met). 'Dear Mr David' = 30 (Mr goes with the surname, not the first name). 'Hi David' or 'Hey Mr Wilson' = 20. A comma after the greeting is optional; assess the greeting, not the comma.

assessment.prompt: You've just sent your team the new price list by email. Write a closing line (the sentence just before Best regards) that invites them to ask questions.
acceptableAnswers: let me know if you have any questions
please let me know if you have any questions
let me know if you have any further questions
please let me know if you have any further questions
if you have any questions please let me know
if you have any questions let me know
let me know if you have questions
feel free to ask if you have any questions
please feel free to ask if you have any questions
please don't hesitate to contact me if you have any questions
please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any questions
let me know if you have any questions about it
let me know if you have any questions about the price list
just let me know if you have any questions
if you have any questions just ask
assessment.rubric: Correct: (Please) let me know if you have any questions. Also full marks: 'Feel free to ask if you have any questions', 'Please don't hesitate to contact me if you have any questions', 'If you have any questions, just ask'. 'Let me know if you have any question' = 80 (any questions, plural). 'If you have questions, ask me.' = 70 (right idea, a bit abrupt). 'Thank you for your attention' = 20 (doesn't invite questions). 'I look forward to hearing from you' = 40 (a real closing line, but it doesn't invite questions).

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: I would like to ask the parking at your hotel.
acceptableAnswers: i would like to ask about the parking at your hotel
i'd like to ask about the parking at your hotel
i would like to ask about parking at your hotel
i'd like to ask about parking at your hotel
assessment.rubric: Correct: I would like to ask about the parking at your hotel (ask about + topic = menanyakan tentang). 'ask for the parking' = 30 (ask for = meminta). 'I want to ask about the parking' = 70 (right fix, but 'want' sounds more demanding than 'would like'). Unchanged = 0.

assessment.prompt: Make this request polite for an email to a supplier. Use Could you: Send me the invoice by Friday.
acceptableAnswers: could you send me the invoice by friday
could you please send me the invoice by friday
could you send me the invoice by friday please
could you send the invoice to me by friday

could you send the invoice to me by friday please

could you send me the invoice by friday if possible
could you please send me the invoice by friday if possible
assessment.rubric: Correct: Could you (please) send me the invoice by Friday(, please)? 'Could you to send' or 'Could you sending' = 40 (could + base verb). 'Could you sent' = 40. 'by Friday' left out = 70 (a clear request says when). 'Can you send me …' = 70 (fine for a colleague, less polite for a supplier, and the task asks for Could you). 'Please send me the invoice by Friday' = 50 (still an order).

assessment.prompt: Complete with the right form of call: I'm in a meeting until 1 p.m. Would you mind ___ me back after lunch?

assessment.rubric: Correct: calling (Would you mind + verb-ing). 'to call' = 20. 'call' = 30. 'called' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Rewrite this sentence for an email to a new client: full words, no chat short forms and no emoji. thx for ur quick reply!! 😊

assessment.prompt: Your Indonesian draft of an email to a hotel ends with 'Terima kasih atas perhatiannya.' Write a natural English thank-you sentence for the end of the email (not 'Thank you for your attention').
acceptableAnswers: thank you for your time
thank you very much for your time
thank you so much for your time
thanks for your time
many thanks for your time
thank you for your help
thank you very much for your help
thank you so much for your help
many thanks for your help
thanks for your help
thank you in advance

thanks in advance
thanks in advance for your help
assessment.rubric: Correct: Thank you (very much) for your time. / Thank you for your help. / Thank you in advance (for your help). 'Thank you for your attention' = 30 (a word-for-word translation: it sounds like the end of a presentation). 'Thank you for your attention and your time' = 60. 'Thanks!' or 'Thx' = 30 (too casual for a hotel).

blocks.text:
In A2 you wrote short messages: a greeting, your news, a question back and an ending. An email to a hotel, a client, a teacher or your boss is **semi-formal** (polite, but not stiff), and it has a few more parts, always in this order:

- **Subject line**: a few words that name the topic: *Question about the TOEIC evening course*
- **Greeting**: *Dear Ms Lestari,*
- **Opening line** with your **purpose** (why you're writing): *I'm writing to ask about your TOEIC evening course.*
- **Body**: the details, in short paragraphs
- a clear **request**: what you want the reader to do, and by when: *Could you send me the timetable, please?*
- **Closing line**: one last friendly sentence: *I look forward to hearing from you.*
- **Sign-off** + your name on a new line: *Best regards, Rina Wulandari*

The reader should know **in the first line** why you're writing.

id.text:
Di pelajaran A2 kamu menulis pesan singkat: salam, kabarmu, pertanyaan balik dan penutup. Email untuk hotel, klien, guru atau atasanmu itu **semi-formal** (setengah resmi: sopan, tapi tidak kaku), dan punya beberapa bagian tambahan, selalu dengan urutan ini:

- **Subject line** (baris subjek): beberapa kata yang menyebut topiknya: *Question about the TOEIC evening course*
- **Greeting** (salam pembuka): *Dear Ms Lestari,*
- **Opening line** (kalimat pembuka) dengan **tujuanmu** (kenapa kamu menulis): *I'm writing to ask about your TOEIC evening course.*
- **Body** (isi): detailnya, dalam paragraf-paragraf pendek
- **request** (permintaan) yang jelas: apa yang kamu ingin pembaca lakukan, dan kapan: *Could you send me the timetable, please?*
- **Closing line** (kalimat penutup): satu kalimat ramah terakhir: *I look forward to hearing from you.*
- **Sign-off** (salam penutup) + namamu di baris baru: *Best regards, Rina Wulandari*

Pembaca harus tahu **di baris pertama** kenapa kamu menulis.

blocks.text: **The subject line is not a greeting, and the purpose comes first.** Many people leave the subject empty or write *Hello* or *URGENT!!!*: the reader can't tell what the email is about. Write 3–8 words that name the topic: *Meeting on Friday: new time*, *Question about my invoice*. Don't put the whole message there. And an Indonesian formal letter often starts slowly (*Dengan hormat, Saya yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini …*) and gives the purpose later. In English, start with it: *I'm writing to …*

id.text: **Baris subjek bukan salam, dan tujuan ditulis paling depan.** Banyak orang mengosongkan subjek atau menulis *Hello* atau *URGENT!!!*: pembaca tidak tahu email itu tentang apa. Tulis 3–8 kata yang menyebut topiknya: *Meeting on Friday: new time*, *Question about my invoice*. Jangan taruh seluruh pesan di sana. Surat resmi bahasa Indonesia juga sering dimulai pelan-pelan (*Dengan hormat, Saya yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini …*) dan tujuannya baru muncul belakangan. Dalam bahasa Inggris, mulai langsung dengan tujuannya: *I'm writing to …*

blocks.prompt: Sari's email to her landlord starts: 'Dear Pak Hartono, My name is Sari. I live in room 4. I usually work from home. I like the building very much. The water heater in my bathroom is broken.' What's the problem?
options: It needs more details about Sari.
blocks.explain: The greeting is fine. But Pak Hartono reads four sentences before he learns why Sari is writing (the broken water heater). Put the purpose first: I'm writing to let you know that the water heater in my bathroom is broken.

id.prompt: Email Sari ke pemilik kosnya dimulai: 'Dear Pak Hartono, My name is Sari. I live in room 4. I usually work from home. I like the building very much. The water heater in my bathroom is broken.' Apa masalahnya?
id.explain: Salamnya sudah benar. Tapi Pak Hartono membaca empat kalimat sebelum tahu kenapa Sari menulis (pemanas airnya rusak). Taruh tujuannya di depan: I'm writing to let you know that the water heater in my bathroom is broken.

id.title: Salam pembuka, kalimat pembuka dan penutup

blocks.text:
**Greeting.** For someone you don't know well: **Dear** + **Mr** (a man) or **Ms** (a woman, said 'miz') + **surname** (nama keluarga: in Western names, usually the last name). Michael Brown → *Dear Mr Brown,* (not *Dear Mr Michael* ✗). **Ms** is safe for any woman, married or not (*Mrs* = a married woman, *Miss* = a young or unmarried woman). Many Indonesian names have no surname, so with Indonesian colleagues *Dear Pak Budi,* / *Dear Bu Ani,* is normal, as in A2. For a friend or a colleague you know well: *Hi Sari,* or *Dear Sari,*. No name at all: *Dear Sir or Madam,* (very formal) or *Dear Customer Service team,*.

**Opening line** (why you're writing):
- *I'm writing to ask about* + a topic: *… to ask about your prices.*
- *I'm writing to let you know that* + a sentence: *… that I can't come on Friday.*
- *I'm writing about* + a topic: *… about my order.*
- When you reply: *Thank you for your email.* / *Thanks for your quick reply.*

**Closing line** (the last sentence):
- *I look forward to hearing from you.* (you want a reply)
- *Let me know if you have any questions.* (you've sent information)
- *Thank you for your help.*

**Sign-off** + your name on a new line: *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,* / *Best wishes,*

id.text:
**Salam pembuka.** Untuk orang yang belum kamu kenal baik: **Dear** + **Mr** (laki-laki) atau **Ms** (perempuan, dibaca 'miz') + **surname** (nama keluarga: pada nama Barat biasanya nama terakhir). Michael Brown → *Dear Mr Brown,* (bukan *Dear Mr Michael* ✗). **Ms** aman untuk semua perempuan, sudah menikah atau belum (*Mrs* = perempuan yang sudah menikah, *Miss* = perempuan muda atau belum menikah). Banyak nama Indonesia tidak punya nama keluarga, jadi dengan rekan kerja orang Indonesia *Dear Pak Budi,* / *Dear Bu Ani,* itu wajar, seperti di A2. Untuk teman atau rekan kerja yang sudah akrab: *Hi Sari,* atau *Dear Sari,*. Kalau tidak tahu namanya sama sekali: *Dear Sir or Madam,* (sangat formal) atau *Dear Customer Service team,*.

**Kalimat pembuka** (kenapa kamu menulis):
- *I'm writing to ask about* + topik: *… to ask about your prices.*
- *I'm writing to let you know that* + kalimat: *… that I can't come on Friday.*
- *I'm writing about* + topik: *… about my order.*
- Saat membalas: *Thank you for your email.* / *Thanks for your quick reply.*

**Kalimat penutup** (kalimat terakhir):
- *I look forward to hearing from you.* (kamu menunggu balasan)
- *Let me know if you have any questions.* (kamu baru mengirim informasi)
- *Thank you for your help.*

**Salam penutup** + namamu di baris baru: *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,* / *Best wishes,*

blocks.text: **Three small traps.** 1) *look forward to* + **-ing**: *I look forward to **hearing** from you*, not *to hear* ✗. This *to* is not the *to* in *want to go*: it works like a small word such as *about*, so the -ing form follows. Just remember the phrase. (*I hope to hear from you soon* is also correct: after *hope to* comes the base verb.) 2) It's **Best regards** with an **s**, not *Best regard* ✗, a very common slip in Indonesian offices. 3) *I am waiting your answer* ✗ (from *Saya menunggu jawaban Anda*) needs *for*, and even *I'm waiting for your answer* sounds impatient: use *I look forward to hearing from you*. British English writes *Mr Brown*, American English *Mr. Brown*: both are correct.

id.text: **Tiga jebakan kecil.** 1) *look forward to* + **-ing**: *I look forward to **hearing** from you*, bukan *to hear* ✗. *to* di sini bukan *to* seperti di *want to go*: fungsinya seperti kata kecil *about*, jadi diikuti bentuk -ing. Ingat saja ungkapannya. (*I hope to hear from you soon* juga benar: setelah *hope to* datang kata kerja dasar.) 2) Yang benar **Best regards** dengan **s**, bukan *Best regard* ✗, kesalahan yang sangat sering muncul di kantor-kantor Indonesia. 3) *I am waiting your answer* ✗ (dari *Saya menunggu jawaban Anda*) butuh *for*, dan *I'm waiting for your answer* pun terdengar tidak sabar: pakai *I look forward to hearing from you*. Bahasa Inggris British menulis *Mr Brown*, Amerika *Mr. Brown*: keduanya benar.

blocks.prompt: Which sign-off is right for an email to a client?
blocks.explain: Kind regards, (or Best regards,) is a polite sign-off for work. Regards always has an s, so 'Best regard' is wrong, and 'Bye bye' is too casual for a client.

id.prompt: Salam penutup mana yang tepat untuk email ke klien?
id.explain: Kind regards, (atau Best regards,) adalah salam penutup yang sopan untuk urusan kerja. Regards selalu pakai s, jadi 'Best regard' salah, dan 'Bye bye' terlalu santai untuk klien.

blocks.text:
In an email the reader can't hear your friendly voice, so an order (*Send me the file.*) or *I want …* can sound rude. Turn the request into a **question** or a soft phrase:

- **Could you** + base verb (kata kerja dasar) …? *Could you send me the timetable, please?* As in A2, *could* here isn't the past: it just sounds softer than *can*.
- **Would you mind** + verb-**ing** …? (= Apakah Anda keberatan …?) *Would you mind checking these numbers?* Remember it as a phrase: after *mind* comes the -ing form. The polite answer *No, not at all* means 'not a problem, I'll do it'.
- **I would like to ask about** + a topic (or *I'd like to ask about*): *I would like to ask about the training schedule.*
- **I'd be grateful if you could** + base verb (= Saya akan sangat berterima kasih jika Anda bisa …): very polite, good for a bigger favour or someone you don't know. *I'd be grateful if you could reply before the weekend.* Remember it as one phrase.

**Softeners** (kata pelunak) make a request sound smaller and kinder: *please*, *just* (*Could you just check the date?*), *a little* (*Could we start a little later?*), *when you have a moment* (kalau Anda sempat), *if possible*. A clear request also says **what** and **when**: *by Thursday*, *before the meeting*.

id.text:
Di email, pembaca tidak bisa mendengar nada suaramu yang ramah, jadi perintah (*Send me the file.*) atau *I want …* bisa terdengar kasar. Ubah permintaanmu menjadi **pertanyaan** atau ungkapan yang lembut:

- **Could you** + kata kerja dasar …? *Could you send me the timetable, please?* Seperti di A2, *could* di sini bukan bentuk lampau: hanya terdengar lebih halus daripada *can*.
- **Would you mind** + kata kerja-**ing** …? (= Apakah Anda keberatan …?) *Would you mind checking these numbers?* Ingat sebagai ungkapan: setelah *mind* datang bentuk -ing. Jawaban sopannya *No, not at all* artinya 'tidak masalah, akan saya lakukan'.
- **I would like to ask about** + topik (atau *I'd like to ask about*): *I would like to ask about the training schedule.*
- **I'd be grateful if you could** + kata kerja dasar (= Saya akan sangat berterima kasih jika Anda bisa …): sangat sopan, cocok untuk bantuan yang lebih besar atau orang yang belum kamu kenal. *I'd be grateful if you could reply before the weekend.* Ingat sebagai satu ungkapan.

**Kata pelunak** membuat permintaan terdengar lebih kecil dan ramah: *please*, *just* (cuma, sebentar: *Could you just check the date?*), *a little* (sedikit: *Could we start a little later?*), *when you have a moment* (kalau Anda sempat), *if possible* (kalau bisa). Permintaan yang jelas juga menyebut **apa** dan **kapan**: *by Thursday*, *before the meeting*.

blocks.text: **Indonesian traps.** 1) *Mohon segera dikirim* is polite in Indonesian, but word for word it becomes an order: *Send me soon* ✗. *Kindly send …*, common in Indonesian offices, is still an order too. Write *Could you send it to me soon, please?* 2) *Saya mau tanya jadwal* → *I want to ask the schedule* ✗. *I want* sounds demanding in a request: use *I would like* / *I'd like*. And to say what your question is about, use **ask about** (= menanyakan tentang): *I'd like to ask about the schedule.* **ask for** = meminta: *I'd like to ask for a copy of the schedule.* So the node's classic mistake *I want to ask the schedule. Send me soon.* becomes **I would like to ask about the schedule. Could you send it to me, please?** (A few short phrases like *ask the price* or *ask the way* are fine as they are.) 3) *Would you mind **to send** …?* ✗ → *Would you mind **sending** …?*

id.text: **Jebakan dari bahasa Indonesia.** 1) *Mohon segera dikirim* itu sopan dalam bahasa Indonesia, tapi kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata jadi perintah: *Send me soon* ✗. *Kindly send …*, yang sering dipakai di kantor-kantor Indonesia, juga tetap perintah. Tulis *Could you send it to me soon, please?* 2) *Saya mau tanya jadwal* → *I want to ask the schedule* ✗. *I want* terdengar menuntut dalam sebuah permintaan: pakai *I would like* / *I'd like*. Dan untuk menyebut topik pertanyaanmu, pakai **ask about** (= menanyakan tentang): *I'd like to ask about the schedule.* **ask for** = meminta: *I'd like to ask for a copy of the schedule.* Jadi kesalahan klasik *I want to ask the schedule. Send me soon.* menjadi **I would like to ask about the schedule. Could you send it to me, please?** (Beberapa ungkapan pendek seperti *ask the price* atau *ask the way* memang sudah benar.) 3) *Would you mind **to send** …?* ✗ → *Would you mind **sending** …?*

blocks.text:
The same news sounds different to your friend and to a client.

**Personal** emails (friends, family): *Hi / Hey*, **contractions** (bentuk singkat: *I'm, can't, don't, I'll*) everywhere, *Thanks so much!*, short sentences, *Can you …?*, an emoji or two, and an ending like *Take care,* / *See you soon,* / *Love,*.

**Semi-formal** emails (your boss, a teacher, a client, a hotel, a company): *Dear …,*, *I hope you are well.*, full words, fewer contractions (with someone new, full forms in the key lines sound careful: *I am writing … I would like …*; with a colleague you know, *I'm* is fine), *Thank you for …*, polite requests, **no emoji** and **no chat short forms** (*thx, pls, btw, u, ur*), and *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,*.

id.text:
Kabar yang sama terdengar berbeda untuk temanmu dan untuk klien.

Email **personal** (teman, keluarga): *Hi / Hey*, **bentuk singkat** (contraction: *I'm, can't, don't, I'll*) di mana-mana, *Thanks so much!*, kalimat pendek, *Can you …?*, satu-dua emoji, dan penutup seperti *Take care,* / *See you soon,* / *Love,*.

Email **semi-formal** (atasan, guru, klien, hotel, perusahaan): *Dear …,*, *I hope you are well.*, kata-kata lengkap, lebih sedikit bentuk singkat (dengan orang baru, bentuk lengkap di kalimat-kalimat penting terdengar lebih rapi: *I am writing … I would like …*; dengan rekan kerja yang sudah kamu kenal, *I'm* boleh), *Thank you for …*, permintaan yang sopan, **tanpa emoji** dan **tanpa singkatan chat** (*thx, pls, btw, u, ur*), serta *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,*.

blocks.text:
**Don't translate Indonesian letter habits.**
- *Kepada Yth. Bapak … / Dengan hormat,* → English has just **one** greeting line: *Dear Pak Hartono,*. There's no English line for *Dengan hormat* (not *With respect,* ✗).
- *Mohon maaf mengganggu waktunya* → usually leave it out. Write *Sorry to bother you* only when you really interrupt someone (on a day off, late at night).
- *Terima kasih atas perhatiannya* → **Thank you for your time.** or *Thank you for your help.* (*Thank you for your attention* sounds like the end of a presentation.)
- *Saya yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini* → leave it out and start with your purpose.
- *Hormat saya,* → *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,*

id.text:
**Jangan menerjemahkan kebiasaan surat bahasa Indonesia.**
- *Kepada Yth. Bapak … / Dengan hormat,* → bahasa Inggris hanya punya **satu** baris salam: *Dear Pak Hartono,*. *Dengan hormat* tidak punya padanan dalam bahasa Inggris (bukan *With respect,* ✗).
- *Mohon maaf mengganggu waktunya* → biasanya tidak perlu ditulis. Tulis *Sorry to bother you* hanya kalau kamu benar-benar mengganggu seseorang (saat hari liburnya, larut malam).
- *Terima kasih atas perhatiannya* → **Thank you for your time.** atau *Thank you for your help.* (*Thank you for your attention* terdengar seperti penutup presentasi.)
- *Saya yang bertanda tangan di bawah ini* → tidak perlu ditulis, langsung mulai dengan tujuanmu.
- *Hormat saya,* → *Best regards,* / *Kind regards,*

assessment.em-1: Kamu menulis email ke manajer sebuah hotel di Bali, Mr David Wilson. Kamu belum pernah bertemu dengannya. Tulis salam pembuka emailmu dalam bahasa Inggris (boleh dengan atau tanpa koma).
assessment.em-2: Kamu baru saja mengirim daftar harga baru ke timmu lewat email. Tulis kalimat penutup dalam bahasa Inggris (kalimat tepat sebelum Best regards) yang mempersilakan mereka bertanya.
assessment.em-3: Perbaiki kesalahannya: I would like to ask the parking at your hotel.
assessment.em-4: Ubah permintaan ini menjadi sopan untuk email ke pemasok. Pakai Could you: Send me the invoice by Friday.
assessment.em-5: Lengkapi dengan bentuk call yang tepat: I'm in a meeting until 1 p.m. Would you mind ___ me back after lunch?
assessment.em-6: Tulis ulang kalimat ini untuk email ke klien baru: kata-kata lengkap, tanpa singkatan chat dan tanpa emoji. thx for ur quick reply!! 😊
assessment.em-7: Draf bahasa Indonesia emailmu ke sebuah hotel diakhiri dengan 'Terima kasih atas perhatiannya.' Tulis kalimat terima kasih yang wajar dalam bahasa Inggris untuk akhir email itu (bukan 'Thank you for your attention').
